claims.claim: LLMs place the major setback and climax earlier in the timeline than human writers, compressing pacing and diminishing suspense and arousal.
claims.source: Are Large Language Models Capable of Generating Human-Level Narratives? (Tian et al.; EMNLP 2024)
claims.quote: introduce plot turning points earlier in the timeline
claims.page: Are Large Language Models Capable of Generating Human-Level Narratives? (Tian et al.; EMNLP 2024)

claims.claim: Models are biased toward certain macro arcs and lack narrative diversity, especially by avoiding negative plot progressions.
claims.source: Are Large Language Models Capable of Generating Human-Level Narratives? (Tian et al.; EMNLP 2024)
claims.quote: particularly in avoiding negative plot progressions
claims.page: Are Large Language Models Capable of Generating Human-Level Narratives? (Tian et al.; EMNLP 2024)

claims.claim: Human stories show higher arousal than LLM stories, and the gap widens after the midpoint toward the ending; explicit turning-point guidance raised suspense ratings ~40%.
claims.source: Are Large Language Models Capable of Generating Human-Level Narratives? (Tian et al.; EMNLP 2024)
claims.page: Are Large Language Models Capable of Generating Human-Level Narratives? (Tian et al.; EMNLP 2024)

claims.claim: As story scale grows (larger maps, more characters), generated plans skip necessary steps while keeping a correct high-level structure.
claims.source: Can LLMs Generate Good Stories? Insights and Challenges from a Narrative Planning Perspective (CoG 2025; Kreminski co-author per his publications page)
claims.quote: output plans tend to skip steps, leading to failure cases
claims.page: Can LLMs Generate Good Stories? Insights and Challenges from a Narrative Planning Perspective (CoG 2025; Kreminski co-author per his publications page)

claims.claim: Most failed plans were causally sound but had characters acting without valid intention — Aladdin obtains the lamp and casts a spell with no established motive.
claims.source: Can LLMs Generate Good Stories? Insights and Challenges from a Narrative Planning Perspective (CoG 2025; Kreminski co-author per his publications page)
claims.page: Can LLMs Generate Good Stories? Insights and Challenges from a Narrative Planning Perspective (CoG 2025; Kreminski co-author per his publications page)

claims.claim: When asked for dramatic conflict, models produced shortcuts such as an adventurer repeatedly getting snakebites and healing himself rather than clashing commitment frames.
claims.source: Can LLMs Generate Good Stories? Insights and Challenges from a Narrative Planning Perspective (CoG 2025; Kreminski co-author per his publications page)
claims.page: Can LLMs Generate Good Stories? Insights and Challenges from a Narrative Planning Perspective (CoG 2025; Kreminski co-author per his publications page)

claims.claim: Intentional-planning success drops sharply from 2 to 3 adventurers and again from 10 to 12, the latter likely from exceeding context limits; only RL-trained reasoning models handled intentionality and conflict.
claims.source: Can LLMs Generate Good Stories? Insights and Challenges from a Narrative Planning Perspective (CoG 2025; Kreminski co-author per his publications page)
claims.page: Can LLMs Generate Good Stories? Insights and Challenges from a Narrative Planning Perspective (CoG 2025; Kreminski co-author per his publications page)

claims.claim: Across 61,608 stories, AI narrators explain the theme in 77% of stories versus 52% human; the pattern is over-determination.
claims.source: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction (Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer, Wieting; 2026)
claims.quote: AI spells out meaning rather than trusting the reader
claims.page: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction (Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer, Wieting; 2026)

claims.claim: AI conveys emotion through physical sensations and bodily metaphors in 81% of stories versus 38% human, and over-uses smell imagery (82% vs 57%).
claims.source: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction (Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer, Wieting; 2026)
claims.quote: physical sensations and bodily metaphors (81% vs. 38% human)
claims.page: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction (Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer, Wieting; 2026)

claims.claim: 79% of AI stories have no subplots versus 57% human; AI favours tighter causal chains and protagonist-driven resolutions (69% vs 46%).
claims.source: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction (Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer, Wieting; 2026)
claims.page: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction (Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer, Wieting; 2026)

claims.claim: AI avoids naming real brands, places or works and uses vague allusions (72% vs 50%); humans cite specific texts and authors at nearly double the rate (47% vs 24%).
claims.source: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction (Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer, Wieting; 2026)
claims.quote: avoids naming real brands, places, or works
claims.page: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction (Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer, Wieting; 2026)

claims.claim: Human stories present morally ambivalent protagonists more often (59% vs 38%), span more locations, and carry more dialogue relative to narration.
claims.source: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction (Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer, Wieting; 2026)
claims.quote: present morally ambivalent protagonists more often (59% vs. 38%)

claims.claim: AI resolutions favour internal understanding or acceptance (47% vs 27% human).
